Keywords: resource limits, oom killed, cpu throttling
Guidance: Pods without CPU/memory requests and limits can starve neighbors or get OOMKilled unpredictably under node pressure.
Do: Set both requests and limits on every container; size requests from observed usage.
Don't: Leave requests/limits unset in production manifests.

Guidance: Confusing liveness and readiness probes causes needless restarts under load; a slow-starting app can be killed by an over-aggressive liveness probe before it's ready.
Do: Use readiness probes to gate traffic and liveness probes only to detect true deadlocks, with generous initialDelaySeconds/failureThreshold.
Don't: Point liveness and readiness at the same endpoint with identical thresholds.

Guidance: Exposing every service as LoadBalancer wastes cloud load balancers and money; most services should be ClusterIP behind a single shared Ingress controller.
Do: Default to ClusterIP + Ingress; reserve LoadBalancer for the ingress controller itself.
Don't: Provision a cloud LoadBalancer per microservice.
Example:
kind: Ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http: {paths: [{path: /, backend: {service: {name: app-svc, port: {number: 80}}}}]}

Guidance: Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default, but they're still the correct place for credentials, not ConfigMaps -- never store passwords or tokens in a ConfigMap.
Do: Store credentials in Secrets and enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration); use ConfigMaps only for non-sensitive settings.
Don't: Put a database password in a ConfigMap because it's easier to edit.

Keywords: hpa, autoscaling, cpu target, scaling thrashing
Guidance: HPA targets set too tight (e.g. 50% CPU with noisy workloads) cause scale up/down thrashing; without stabilization windows pods flap under bursty traffic.
Do: Set realistic target utilization (typically 60-80%) and configure behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds to prevent flapping.
Don't: Leave HPA on default behavior with a tight CPU target on a spiky workload.

Keywords: pdb, voluntary eviction, node drain, availability
Guidance: Without a PodDisruptionBudget, a node drain or cluster upgrade can evict all replicas of a deployment simultaneously, causing an outage during routine maintenance.
Do: Define a PDB with minAvailable or maxUnavailable for every multi-replica deployment.
Don't: Rely on replica count alone to survive node drains.

Keywords: network policy, default deny, lateral movement, pod-to-pod
Guidance: Without NetworkPolicies, every pod in a cluster can talk to every other pod by default, letting a single compromised pod move laterally across the whole namespace.
Do: Apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace, then explicitly allow required ingress/egress paths.
Don't: Leave namespaces with no NetworkPolicy in a multi-tenant cluster.

Guidance: Binding cluster-admin to a workload's ServiceAccount (common in quick demos) gives that pod full API server control if compromised.
Do: Grant the minimum verbs/resources needed via a scoped Role/RoleBinding in the workload's own namespace.
Don't: Bind cluster-admin to a default ServiceAccount for convenience.

Guidance: Without a ResourceQuota, one team's namespace can consume unbounded cluster CPU/memory/object count, starving every other tenant on shared infrastructure.
Do: Set a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange per namespace in multi-tenant clusters.
Don't: Assume individual pod limits are enough to protect the cluster as a whole.

Guidance: Default rolling-update settings can still cause capacity dips or overly slow rollouts; maxUnavailable=0 with maxSurge tuned keeps full capacity during deploys at the cost of extra pods briefly.
Do: Set maxUnavailable: 0 and a sane maxSurge for user-facing services that can't tolerate a capacity dip.
Don't: Accept default rollingUpdate values without checking they match the service's availability requirements.

Guidance: StatefulSet pods each need their own stable PVC via volumeClaimTemplates -- reusing a single shared PVC across replicas breaks stateful workloads like databases.
Do: Use volumeClaimTemplates so each StatefulSet replica gets its own PVC with a stable name (data-mysql-0, data-mysql-1...).
Don't: Mount one shared PVC across all StatefulSet replicas expecting per-instance data.

Guidance: Without affinity/taint rules, the scheduler can co-locate noisy or incompatible workloads (e.g. GPU jobs on non-GPU nodes' neighbors) or place pods on nodes meant to stay dedicated.
Do: Use taints on specialized nodes (e.g. GPU, spot) and matching tolerations + nodeAffinity on the pods meant to run there.
Don't: Rely on default scheduling for workloads that need dedicated or excluded node pools.
Example: tolerations:\n- {key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule}

Keywords: imagepullpolicy, latest tag, image pull, mutable image
Guidance: Using the :latest tag with imagePullPolicy: Always makes deployments non-reproducible -- the same manifest can pull a different image content over time, breaking rollbacks.
Do: Pin images to immutable digests or versioned tags, and use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent except for genuinely mutable dev tags.
Don't: Deploy production workloads on the :latest tag.

Keywords: kubectl describe, kubectl logs, crashloopbackoff, debug pod
Guidance: Jumping straight to kubectl delete pod on a failing pod destroys the evidence; describe/logs/events/ephemeral-debug-containers in that order usually finds root cause fast.
Do: Run kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs --previous before restarting, and use kubectl debug for ephemeral troubleshooting containers.
Don't: Delete and let a failing pod restart before reading its events and logs.

Keywords: helm values, helm chart, values.yaml, environment overrides
Guidance: Hardcoding environment-specific values inside a shared Helm chart template forces chart edits per environment; layered values files (values.yaml + values-prod.yaml) keep the chart generic.
Do: Keep a base values.yaml and override with environment-specific -f values-<env>.yaml files at install time.
Don't: Fork the chart per environment to change a handful of values.
